Existing datasets and benchmarks differ from real long-horizon failures in three ways. (1) Coverage. Most datasets contain only perfect trajectories; those that contain errors take them from human demo errors, injected errors, or self-reported failures, and these are mostly low-level execution errors such as invalid clicks ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Jung et al., 2026 ) . We annotated the 619 failures of six agents in CUA-Recovery-Test and found that real errors lie mostly in decisions: planning and perception account for 57.3% of root causes, whereas execution errors account for 84.3% of AgentNet and 71.2% of GUI-Reflection root causes (Figure 3 a). (2) Horizon. Existing trajectories are short, and their errors are visible at the step they occur, while 78.1% of the errors we annotated surface three or more steps after the root cause, with a median of 17 steps (Figure 3 b). (3) Interface. Real computer work is hybrid: agents inspect visual state through the GUI and run precise, bulk operations through the command line, both on the same application state. Existing resources fall short of this setting in two ways. First, training data contain mostly GUI actions (Table 1 ), so a model trained on them rarely sees the two interfaces used together. Second, scoring often relies on screenshots, yet frontier agents prefer the command line when it is available and produce few or no screenshots. On MyPCBench, once the judge reads terminal output, tool-call responses, GUI action logs, and screenshots together, GPT 5.5 rises from the officially reported 45.1% Perfect Pass ( Jang et al., 2026a ) to 85.0% Pass@3. Screenshot-based scoring therefore underestimates such agents and cannot compare agents that interact in different ways on equal terms. Figure 2: Overview of our methodology and benchmark. These three gaps motivate our work. Firstly, we propose CUA-Recovery , a benchmark for error recovery in long-horizon computer use (Figure 2 ). Its test set, CUA-Recovery-Test, contains 2,250 human-verified erroneous states over 100 tasks, drawn from 619 failed rollouts of six agents. An agent takes over each state 0 to 25 steps after the root cause and is not told that an error occurred. We report whether it notices the inherited error (Error-Awareness Rate, EAR), how much of the task it completes (Rubric Score), and whether the task is completed in any one of three runs (Pass@3). The judge reads terminal output, tool calls, and screenshots together, so agents that act through the GUI and the command line are scored on equal terms. Its training set, CUA-Recovery-Train, contains 8.6K verified recovery trajectories over 377 tasks. Secondly, we build CUA-Recovery with ReRail , a framework that synthesizes recovery data from real failures. ReRail converts each seed task into an executable intermediate representation whose gold lineage fixes the correct value at every step, and composes these tasks into long multi-application workflows over shared persistent state. The gold lineage removes the need to inject errors. Several agents execute the workflows through GUI and CLI; ReRail keeps only the failures that the task verifier confirms, locates each root cause against the gold lineage, and cuts the rollout at several depths after it. Every erroneous state thus comes from an agent’s own decision, and its takeover depth is controlled. For training, the base model, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, continues from each cut under hints of increasing specificity. A continuation is kept only if the verifier confirms that it completes the task, and the hint is then removed, so the model learns to notice and repair the error without being told. On CUA-Recovery-Test, Pass@3 reaches at most 25.5% across six agents and all takeover depths, and clean-start success does not imply recovery: Kimi-K3 solves 66.9% of MyPCBench tasks from scratch but notices at most 18.5% of the errors in its own failures. Notably, training on CUA-Recovery-Train narrows this gap. The ReRail-35B-A3B recovers better than its base model, surpasses Kimi-K3 on Kimi-K3’s own failures at early takeover depths, and raises clean-start Pass@3 from 9.2% to 24.5% on MyPCBench and from 24.1% to 34.9% on Odysseys. In summary, our contributions are: • CUA-Recovery , an evaluation and training benchmark built from real policy-induced failures in long, stateful computer-use workflows, with 2,250 human-verified test states and 8.6K verified recovery trajectories in training set. • ReRail , a pipeline that composes seed tasks into long workflows with gold lineage and turns verifier-confirmed agent failures into test states and verified recoveries. • A controlled study showing that strong clean-start performance does not imply reliable recovery, and that fine-tuning on CUA-Recovery-Train improves both recovery and clean-start performance. 2 Related Work Long-Horizon Benchmarks for Robust CUAs. CUA benchmarks measure grounding ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , step accuracy on offline trajectories ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025c ) , and end-to-end success in live environments ( Bonatti et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ) . Recent benchmarks extend the horizon: MyPCBench ( Jang et al., 2026a ) builds persona-grounded workflows over persistent multi-application state, OSWorld 2.0 ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) collects tasks that take a human more than an hour, and Agents’ Last Exam ( Sun et al., 2026b ) covers professional workflows across 55 subfields. These benchmarks report task success and partial credit. Robustness benchmarks apply an externally designed stressor, such as perturbations and injected faults ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Sun et al., 2026a ) or adversarial content ( Liao et al., 2025 ) ; AgentErrorBench ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) analyzes failures of text-based LLM agents. Closest to our work, Bu et al. (2026) study recovery from policy-induced errors on short-horizon GUI tasks; as their data are unreleased, we compare with their reported statistics (Figure 3 a). CUA-Recovery measures whether an agent detects and repairs a real error after taking over mid-task: it draws erroneous states from the agents’ own long-horizon failures and places the takeover point up to 25 steps after the root cause, beyond the agents’ visual context. Data for Training Robust CUAs. CUAs are trained on human demonstrations ( Rawles et al., 2023 ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) and synthesized trajectories ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Pahuja et al., 2025 ; Trabucco et al., 2025 ; Gandhi & Neubig, 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Jung et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and learn error handling from reflection data and critics ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Wanyan et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2025 ) , self-training on failed trajectories ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , or online RL ( Bai et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025a ; Lu et al., 2025b ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . Public corpora are short: AgentNet averages 18.8 steps with 7.2% multi-application trajectories, ProCUA-SFT 29.7 steps with 26.1%, and GUI-Reflection 3.8 steps, and none carries persistent state across applications (Table 1 ). CUA-Recovery-Train averages 60.0 steps with 67.5% multi-application trajectories, and pairs real failures of several policies with verifier-accepted recoveries. 3 Problem Formulation Environment and tasks. CUA-Recovery addresses the three gaps in Section 1 : its errors come from the agents’ own policies rather than injection (coverage), propagate through dependencies across applications and stay hidden for many steps (horizon), and arise in a persistent desktop environment where agents act through both GUI and CLI (interface). ReRail composes seed tasks into long multi-application workflows, collects failures from multiple agents, and turns them into CUA-Recovery-Test, a human-verified test set of 2,250 erroneous states, and CUA-Recovery-Train, a training set of 8,577 verified recovery trajectories. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline. 4.1 Building the Benchmark with ReRail The key idea of ReRail is that every task carries a gold lineage, the correct value at every step. An agent’s own failure can then be traced against this lineage to locate its root cause, so no errors need to be injected. We outline the main steps below; Appendix B gives the details. Building tasks with dependencies. We start from the tasks in MyPCBench ( Jang et al., 2026a ) . For each task, ReRail creates an executable intermediate representation that records the application operations, the data they read and write, and the checks on their outputs. Running this graph on a fresh environment snapshot gives the expected intermediate values and final state. To form longer workflows, we connect two tasks when the output of the first can serve as an input to the second. A value that was given in the original instruction must now be found through earlier work, creating a dependency along which a mistake can spread. The resulting pool contains 477 workflows, with medians of three source tasks and 22 graph nodes per workflow. Checking the generated tasks. We execute each workflow to obtain its reference intermediate values and final state, then freeze its verifiers to this gold lineage. We perturb intermediate values and rerun the workflow; a mutation is caught if a downstream verifier fails or if the final outputs or stored data differ from the gold lineage. We retain workflows that catch at least half of the executed mutations and select tasks across different dependency lengths. Constructing erroneous states and the evaluation suite. We split the composed workflows into training and test tasks, with all rollouts, takeover states, and recovery trajectories derived from the same workflow assigned to one split. We run six agents on the workflows: GPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Kimi-K3, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, EvoCUA-32B, and OpenCUA-72B. For each failed rollout, ReRail compares the recorded execution with the gold lineage to identify the root-cause step t r t_{r} , the error type, and the first step at which the error becomes evident. To keep each case controlled, experts fix any unrelated mistakes before t r t_{r} , so that the root cause is the only error in the prefix. ReRail then creates takeover states by replaying the rollout to depths d ∈ { 0 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 , 25 } d\in\{0,5,10,15,20,25\} after the root cause. Each replay must reproduce the state recorded at the same point in the original rollout. For the test suite, human annotators verify the root cause, error type, error horizon, repaired prefix, and replayed state. These annotations support the awareness metric and analyses by error type and horizon (Appendix E ). Generating the training suite. For each erroneous state in the training split, the base model, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, attempts to complete the task with guidance about the earlier error. Recovery generation begins with a hint that identifies the erroneous step, then adds the conflicting evidence and the affected data if earlier attempts fail. The first continuation accepted by the final verifier becomes the training target; a teacher model is used when the base model produces no verified continuation. Each training example contains the task instruction, the erroneous history, and the verified continuation. The hints are omitted from the training input, matching the unaware takeover setting used for evaluation. Appendix F.4 describes the hint schedule and generation budget. 4.2 Dataset Composition and Analysis Evaluation at different takeover depths. At each test state, an agent receives the task and the preceding interaction history, then continues without an error warning. The six takeover depths cover histories in which the root-cause screenshot is recent, near the 20-screenshot context limit, or outside that limit. The test set contains 602, 443, 373, 328, 273, and 231 states at depths d = 0 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 , 25 d=0,5,10,15,20,25 , respectively. The number of eligible cases decreases with depth; the replay and eligibility rules are described in Appendix C.1 . Training and test suites. Table 7 summarizes the two splits. The training suite provides examples of how to finish a task after an error; the test suite provides replayable states and human-checked labels for measuring error awareness and recovery. These labels also let us examine what kinds of errors agents make and how long those errors remain hidden before becoming evident. Errors beyond individual actions. Most failures in CUA-Recovery are wrong decisions, not wrong clicks. They span planning, progress and state perception, execution, and termination errors. Examples include choosing records from the wrong year, reading a quantity incorrectly and using it in an order, and creating events in the wrong calendar application (Appendix C.4.1 ). These cases require the agent to check earlier decisions and the data they produced. Planning and perception account for 57.3% of root causes, termination for 23.5%, and execution for 19.1%. For comparison, the available estimates for AgentNet and GUI-Reflection assign 84.3% and 71.2% to execution errors (Figure 3 a). Errors that become clear later. Most errors surface only at the end of a rollout. In 602 of the 619 labeled failures, the error becomes explicit within the recorded rollout, and in 361 of them (60.0%), the evidence first appears at the final step. The median delay from the root cause is 17 steps, and 78.1% of errors surface at least three steps later. This gives CUA-Recovery a substantial set of failures in which recovery requires revisiting earlier work. We evaluate GPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Kimi-K3, EvoCUA-32B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and OpenCUA-72B. Agents use their respective scaffolds; EvoCUA and OpenCUA use GUI actions only, while the other configurations expose command-line tools where supported (Appendix F ). In self-takeover, each agent resumes states drawn from its own failures. It receives the recorded history without an error warning and can take up to 100 additional steps. Error-Awareness Rate (EAR) measures whether an agent explicitly recognizes a problem in the inherited work. Rubric Score, defined in Section 3 , measures partial task completion, while Pass@3 reports full completion in at least one of three runs. Reporting them together separates expressed awareness from recovery outcomes. Clean-start evaluation. We also run agents from the initial task state on MyPCBench ( Jang et al., 2026a ) and Odysseys ( Jang et al., 2026b ) , with 184 and 200 tasks, respectively. Each run is limited to 150 steps and 3,600 seconds. MyPCBench supplies the source tasks used to build our workflows and measures clean-start performance in the source environment. Odysseys contains live-web tasks outside the training environment and measures whether the effect of recovery training extends to a different task setting. 5.2 Benchmarking Recovery on CUA-Recovery-Test We let each of the six agents take over states from its own failures at six diverse takeover depths. Table 2 reports EAR, Rubric Score, and Pass@3. These results lead to four findings as followed. Finding 1: Current agents rarely recover completely from their own failures. Complete recovery is difficult for all six agents on CUA-Recovery-Test. Across all agents and takeover depths, Pass@3 reaches at most 25.5%, achieved by GPT 5.5 at d = 20 d=20 (Table 16 ). Claude Opus 4.8 reaches at most 7.7%, while none of the three open-source agents exceeds 6.4%. These results show that even strong computer-use agents often fail to complete a task once an earlier error has affected the workflow. Finding 2: Clean-start performance does not reliably predict error awareness. Kimi-K3 achieves 66.9% Pass@3 on MyPCBench from a clean start, but recognizes only 7.8–18.5% of the inherited errors in its own failures. In contrast, OpenCUA-72B achieves 5.1% clean-start Pass@3 but recognizes 14.1–26.1% of its inherited errors (Tables 3 and 2 ). Finding 3: Recognizing an error rarely leads to recovery. Across the self-takeover runs of all six agents, EAR reaches at most 44.0% and remains below 33% for all agents except Claude Opus 4.8 (Table 2 ). We next group each agent’s individual runs by whether it recognizes the inherited error and compute verifier success within each group. Macro-averaged across the six agents, the verifier pass rate is 15.6 % 15.6\% for aware runs and 12.2 % 12.2\% for unaware runs (Appendix Table 18 ). Most runs still fail after recognizing the error: agents often identify a problem but leave the affected state unchanged or fail to repair all of its consequences. In unaware runs, agents almost always continue from the inherited state without revisiting the earlier work. Awareness is therefore associated with a greater chance of recovery, but recognition alone is rarely sufficient. Finding 4: Later takeovers remain difficult even when awareness improves. From d = 20 d=20 to d = 25 d=25 , the root-cause screenshot moves beyond the 20-screenshot history. Over this interval, GPT 5.5’s EAR rises from 16.2% to 21.0%, while its Pass@3 falls from 25.5% to 18.9%. Claude’s EAR also rises, from 18.8% to 27.3%, while Pass@3 falls from 7.7% to 0.0%. For Kimi-K3, Pass@3 falls from 23.1% to 9.1%. This pattern suggests a trade-off at later takeover points. As an error propagates through the workflow, its effects become more visible in the current state, making the problem easier to notice. Once the root-cause screenshot leaves the context window, however, the agent must infer how the problem began from its downstream effects, making the error harder to diagnose and repair. Existing data and benchmarks miss this setting in three ways: errors are injected or low-level rather than agent-induced, trajectories are too short for errors to stay hidden, and evaluation covers only GUI actions with screenshot-based scoring. We present CUA-Recovery, a benchmark built with ReRail from agents’ own failures in long multi-application workflows involving both GUI and CLI, with a human-verified test set and verified recovery trajectories for training. Fine-tuning on CUA-Recovery-Train improves recovery from inherited errors and clean-start performance, including in an unseen environment, suggesting that learning from real failures is a practical path toward reliable computer-use agents. Although the current MyPCBench task set offers realistic workflows, most of the tasks are relatively short, requiring only 20 to 45 steps for a capable agent to complete, and the dependency structures that allow errors to remain hidden typically span no more than two nodes. Studying hidden errors at scale requires tasks whose dependency chains are long and whose ground truth is executable, so that every intermediate value, every written cell, and the final state are known before any agent runs, properties that current benchmarks lack. We therefore synthesize tasks by composing verified source tasks and accept a composition only after it has been executed and its verifiers have been shown to reject wrong runs. This appendix describes the pipeline as implemented: the extraction of an executable task representation from each source task (§ B.2 ), the composition search with an executable gate (§ B.3 ), verifier freezing and the mutation test that measures verifier coverage (§ B.4 ), horizon-controlled selection with world and instruction variants (§ B.5 ), and the scale and horizon of the released set (§ B.6 ). A task is represented as a grounded DAG M = ( V , E ) M=(V,E) over one frozen environment snapshot. Every node v ∈ V v\in V records the application it acts on, and its operation is selected from the following action set: retrieve, resolve, filter, compare, aggregate, verify, decide, create, modify, delete, communicate, confirm. It also defines the table cells it reads, the values it produces along with an executable derivation, such as a read-only SQL query, an expression over upstream values, a file read, or a row or file creation, the cells it writes, its reversibility class, and a node verifier. An edge transfers a value or state from an output port to an input port; if no edge connects to a specific input port, that port holds the literal or constant specified in the instruction. The graph carries a final-state verifier with an explicit set of equivalent final states. The snapshot consists of 17 application databases with 201 tables, a schema graph that captures both foreign-key and inferred relationships, and an inventory of the 48 documents in the persona’s home directory. The file inventory is exposed as a single virtual table, allowing files and database rows to be treated as the same kind of fact. Extraction and programmatic validation. A language model extracts the Task IR of each of the 184 MyPCBench source tasks from the instruction, the rubric, the persona, and the schema. The result is validated programmatically rather than by an LLM judge. Static checks verify that the DAG is valid, that every cell is grounded in the schema graph, and that every named entity exists in the snapshot. Each input literal must either appear in the instruction or refer to the persona’s own identity, ensuring that facts the agent is expected to retrieve are not provided directly as constants. The gold IR is then executed on a fresh copy of the snapshot. The interpreter evaluates each derivation, performs the declared writes, checks the cells actually read by each SQL query against the declared reads, and aborts if it encounters an undeclared write. It also records the gold lineage G ⁡ ( M ) G(M) , including every produced value, every written cell, and the state digest after each node. Finally, the gold values are compared with the ground truth in the source rubric, such as amounts, dates, and names. Relative-date variables are expanded using the snapshot’s reference time. When a rubric contains no comparable literals, it is evaluated based on the overlap between its wording and the gold values. Any task that fails validation is re-extracted with the program’s findings appended to the prompt, for up to four rounds. We finally accepted 135 of 184 tasks (73.4%) from the original MyPCBench, based on the validation situation: 53 by literal agreement with the rubric and 82 by wording. Of the 49 remaining tasks, 34 cannot be executed because the model’s derivations or writes are incompatible with the actual schema, 8 have rubrics that contain no comparable values, 5 have final verifiers that reject their own gold runs, and 2 contradict their rubrics. The accepted IRs have a median of 6 nodes. Every accepted IR ships with its gold lineage, which is the single source of truth for everything that follows. Operators and search. For each seed IR, we consider beam search for compositions with any IR in the accepted pool. At each step, the search can pass an output of task A A to a literal input of task B B , add another instance of the same operation pattern, attach an additional producer to a comparison or aggregation node, reuse a value several nodes after it is produced, or use a boolean produced by a decide node in A A to guard the first state-changing node in B B . The resulting graph is re-evaluated after each step. To avoid naming conflicts, each node identifier is prefixed with its parent task. The provenance record for each composition stores the operator, the port binding, and the source tasks. Before execution, each candidate must pass a set of static checks. A graph is rejected if more than 25% of it consists of independent components, which usually indicates that two tasks have been placed side by side rather than meaningfully combined. It is also rejected if a value passed from one task to another has no effect on later computation, if fewer than two nodes fall within the target horizon range (§ B.5 ), or if the graph contains fewer than 10 or more than 24 nodes. The lower bound excludes tasks that are too short to meaningfully test long-horizon reasoning (§ B.6 ). The upper bound keeps tasks within reach of current agents. Candidates that survive these checks are executed on a fresh copy of the snapshot. The execution must complete successfully, and the final verifier must accept the resulting gold state. The beam retains 16 states, allows at most three grafts, and uses no more than 48 gold executions for each seed in each round. A full copy of every database is used for each world, so recomputing all database digests after every step would be expensive. Instead, the interpreter caches the digest of each database and recomputes it only when the corresponding connection reports a change. This reduces the time required for one gold execution from 8.9 s to 0.1 s, making executable validation practical. Composed rubrics. For a workflow composed from source tasks T 1 , … , T k T_{1},\ldots,T_{k} , we form its rubric by combining the rubric items of the source tasks. When composition replaces a source-task input with an upstream output, we update the corresponding expected values and verification descriptions using the composed gold lineage. Each retained item keeps its source-task weight. The resulting rubric is used both to construct the frozen programmatic verifier and, item by item, by the GPT 5.6-Terra rubric judge. To quantify how deeply an error can hide before being exposed, we compute the static latent horizon λ ⁡ ( v ) \lambda(v) on the IR prior to execution. Axis 1: World variants. Once base tasks are selected, we introduce environmental hazards as the first dimension of variation. These hazards include identity aliases, stale documents, title-similar distractor events, and broken preconditions. To prevent artificial over-injection, we first query each hazard’s baseline occurrence rate in the snapshot. We inject a hazard only if its baseline rate is non-zero, capping the post-injection rate at twice the baseline. When a node’s instruction constant or output matches the hazard selector, the environment seeder applies the hazard as a persona patch. In our snapshot, only distractor events met these conditions (baseline count: 19), whereas identity aliases and stale documents did not qualify for injection. Axis 2: Instruction variants. Instruction realization forms the second dimension of variation. For each selected task, the model generates candidate instructions from the graph summary and public context without revealing restricted “hidden values”, which are gold values excluded from initial inputs and prior seeds. An instruction is retained only if it contains all required input literals without leaking hidden values. Distinct valid instructions yield independent rollout starting points while retaining the task’s core gold target and verifiers.
